Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: Ronald, a 63-year-old financial analyst from New Zealand, had always found solace in the predictability of numbers and the stability of his life. Married for over thirty years, he had built a comfortable life with his wife, Emma, in a quiet suburban neighborhood. However, everything changed one fateful evening three years ago when he was involved in a life-threatening car accident. The details remained etched in his mind as if they were happening again: the screeching tires, the smell of burnt rubber mingling with the metallic scent of blood, and the darkness that enveloped him as he lost consciousness. Since that traumatic night, Ronald's world had become increasingly restrictive. He found himself grappling with a powerful array of triggers that erupted without warning, sending him spiraling back to that dark moment. The mere sound of a car rattling past could send his heart racing, a visceral reminder of the chaos he had endured. With every jolt of anxiety that came from those sounds, Ronald's conviction that he was perpetually at risk grew stronger, leading him to believe that he must always be on guard against an imminent threat. Each time he felt that anxiety, it would trigger vivid memories of the accident, as the sound of screeching tires pulled him right back into the chaos of that night, making him relive the terror he had experienced. With each trigger, Ronald found himself thinking that he was weak and vulnerable, leading him to interpret these moments as signs that he would never escape the fear that dominated his life. With every trigger, Ronald became more convinced that he was weak and vulnerable, leading him to interpret each incident as a sign that he was incapable of protecting himself, which only deepened his negative appraisals. Each time a sound triggered his anxiety, it served to drag up the vivid memories of the accident, as if the echo of the screeching tires was a direct line back to the chaos he had experienced, reinforcing the belief that danger was ever-present. He could still smell the oil and gasoline from the accident scene during moments of quiet, and even the faintest whiff could transport him back to the terror he felt, making it impossible to distinguish between past and present. Once these memories surfaced, they heightened his sense of threat, as he felt the danger from that night was not just a memory but an ever-present risk lurking nearby. Each time the smell hit him, it triggered a flood of memories from that night, bringing back the vivid sensations of fear and chaos, as if he was reliving the accident all over again. It was a constant battle; every time he encountered darkness-whether it be a dimly lit room or the shadows of night-he felt a suffocating sense of dread wash over him. The shadows whispered of vulnerability, and he was unable to shake the feeling that he might be trapped again. Each trigger only reinforced Ronald's negative appraisals. He had come to believe that he must remain hypervigilant at all times, convinced that danger lurked around every corner, waiting to pounce. This belief led him to constantly scan his environment for potential triggers, as he felt that if he let his guard down, he might inadvertently invite danger back into his life. This entrenched belief made every unfamiliar situation feel like a potential threat, leading him to interpret benign events through a lens of danger, thus heightening his sense of vulnerability. The constant awareness of his perceived vulnerability meant that almost any ambiguous situation triggered a cascade of anxiety, as if he were always scanning for signs of danger lurking just out of sight. His negative appraisal that he was weak and vulnerable meant that he viewed every new situation as a test he was destined to fail, which only served to amplify his sense of threat in those moments. This belief made him feel as though he was always on the brink of danger, heightening his anxiety and making him hyper-vigilant to any cues that could indicate a threat, reinforcing the cycle of fear. His belief that he was vulnerable meant that he approached each day with a sense of dread, as though he carried an invisible weight that amplified his fears, making every unfamiliar situation a potential trigger for disaster. This conviction that he was perpetually at risk heightened his sense of threat, making it feel as though danger lurked just beyond his awareness, ready to pounce at any moment. If he allowed himself to think about the accident, he feared he would unravel completely, so he avoided those thoughts at all costs. His negative appraisal that he was weak and vulnerable kept bringing forth memories of the crash, as if he needed to constantly remind himself of his perceived failure to protect himself, making those memories more accessible and distressing. The conviction that he was forever changed meant that those memories often surged to the forefront of his mind, replaying the accident in vivid detail and amplifying his feelings of inadequacy. He would often scan rooms for exits as soon as he entered, a habit that had developed in the wake of the accident. This habit stemmed from his belief that he was always at risk, which heightened his sensitivity to potential triggers in his environment, making him hyper-aware of anything that could signal danger. He was certain that he had to be especially careful because, in his mind, it was only a matter of time before something else went wrong. This constant vigilance turned his home into a fortress, and he found himself checking locks multiple times each night, waking up in a cold sweat to ensure that he was safe. The toll it took on his marriage was palpable; Emma would often look at him with concern, unsure of how to reach the man she once knew. Ronald's memories of the accident felt so immediate that he could hardly breathe when they surfaced. He would hear the echoes of the tires screeching and the shattering glass, and it was as if he were reliving the experience in real-time. These memories, once they surfaced, intensified his sense of threat, as if the danger from that night had not only happened but was still a part of his present reality, lurking just out of sight. Whenever those memories broke through, they left him feeling hunted, with the past invading his thoughts and reinforcing the belief that he was still in danger, unable to escape the shadows of his trauma. Once those memories resurfaced, they intensified his sense of threat, making him feel as though the danger he had experienced was not merely a past event but an ongoing reality that he could not escape. Once the memories emerged, they not only brought back the fear of the accident but also reinforced his feeling of being hunted, making danger feel immediate and inescapable. These memories often invaded his thoughts during everyday moments, triggered by the faintest sound or smell that reminded him of that night. He would sit at his desk, trying to focus on financial reports, but the auditory recall of the accident would pull him away, leaving him disoriented and rattled. The memories were not just recollections; they were visceral experiences that heightened his sense of threat, amplifying the belief that he was in constant danger. In his attempt to cope, Ronald found himself trapped in a cycle where triggers led to negative appraisals, which in turn fed into his sense of threat. As he navigated this cycle, each new reminder of his trauma brought forth memories that were both vivid and distressing, further entrenching him in the belief that he was doomed to relive the past. The constant anticipation of danger made even the most mundane situations feel fraught with risk, as if the shadows whispered reminders of his past trauma and his inability to escape it. The more he tried to avoid thinking about the accident, the more powerful the memories became, creating a loop that tightened around him. The memories that surfaced in this context reinforced his sense of threat, making him feel as if he were not just recalling the past but experiencing it anew, thus feeding into his anxiety and urgency to avoid triggers. He felt as though he were living in a cage, constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger. This constant state of heightened alertness not only drained his energy but also made it even harder to keep the traumatic memories at bay, as the fear of danger seemed to awaken those vivid recollections anew. This constant vigilance heightened his sense of threat, as if the very act of being on high alert fed the narrative that he was indeed always in danger, making even the most mundane situations feel fraught with risk. His belief that danger was ever-present kept the traumatic memories alive and vivid, as if they were perpetually ready to invade his thoughts, further intertwining his sense of threat with the recollections of that night. Each day passed with an undercurrent of anxiety, and he struggled to find peace in a life that had once felt so safe and predictable. With every moment filled with anxiety, even the smallest triggers felt like warnings, reaffirming his belief that safety was an illusion and that he was always on the brink of another catastrophe. Finally, after years of enduring this torment, Ronald decided it was time to seek help. He realized that the persistent sense of threat he carried only compounded his memories of the accident, making him feel trapped in a cycle he desperately wanted to break before it consumed him entirely. He felt a deep fear that without intervention, the memories and the threat they carried would continue to dominate his life, leaving him trapped in a cycle of dread and avoidance. This ongoing sense of threat acted like a magnet for his memories, pulling them into the forefront of his mind and making every day feel like a reminder of his past trauma, reinforcing his belief that he was always on the brink of another catastrophe. Sitting in his therapist's office, he revealed his fears and frustrations, expressing a deep yearning for the freedom to live without the shadows of the past clinging to him. What frightened him most was the possibility that he would never reclaim the life he once had, or that he would inadvertently push Emma away in his relentless pursuit of safety. Yet, nestled within his fear was a flicker of hope-that perhaps, with the right support, he could find a way to navigate through the darkness and back into the light of his life. After the memory broke through, it left him with the unsettling belief that the danger he had faced was still present, causing his heart to race as if he were reliving the terror all over again.

This constant vigilance turned his home into a fortress, and he found himself checking locks multiple times each night, waking up in a cold sweat to ensure that he was safe. He would hear the echoes of the tires screeching and the shattering glass, and it was as if he were reliving the experience in real-time. The memories were not just recollections; they were visceral experiences that heightened his sense of threat, amplifying the belief that he was in constant danger.

In his attempt to cope, Ronald found himself trapped in a cycle where triggers led to negative appraisals, which in turn fed into his sense of threat. The more he tried to avoid thinking about the accident, the more powerful the memories became, creating a loop that tightened around him.   e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."

  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
